claims.text: The starting material is bulk HfNbTaTiZr in an as-cast or annealed state.
High-energy neutron or ion irradiation is the proposed intervention.
High-energy particle irradiation will introduce lattice defects into bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
The irradiation-induced defects will include vacancies, interstitials, and dislocation loops.
Irradiation should be performed between room temperature and 500 °C.
The proposed irradiation fluence is 10^16 to 10^18 particles/cm^2.
Irradiation-induced lattice defects will scatter phonons.
Phonon scattering by the defects will reduce phonon mean free paths.
Reducing phonon mean free paths will decrease the lattice contribution to thermal conductivity.
Irradiation will reduce the lattice thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr by 10–50% relative to unchanged material.
The magnitude of the reduction will depend on irradiation fluence and irradiation temperature.
The prediction applies to measurements between 300 and 1200 K.
The prediction applies for irradiation fluences up to 10^18 particles/cm^2.
Previous studies provide a thermal-conductivity baseline for unchanged bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
The 3ω method can be used to measure thermal conductivity as a function of temperature.
TEM or XRD can confirm the introduction of irradiation-induced lattice defects.
Failure of total thermal conductivity to decrease after irradiation would falsify the lattice-thermal-conductivity hypothesis.
Failure to confirm the introduction of lattice defects would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The prediction concerns the lattice contribution specifically, but the experiment and falsification rule use total thermal conductivity without an electrical-resistivity or other measurement that separates electronic and lattice contributions. An unchanged total conductivity therefore would not decisively contradict the stated lattice-specific outcome.
